Holding on until the last moment

"To be honest, we held on until the very last moment." Ms. Yuen and her older sister grew up with their parents at Wang Fuk Court. Their father later passed away and her sister got married, so Ms. Yuen and her mother lived together until the fire. Her mother perished in the blaze. During the past period of moving upstairs, she once wore a hand-written sweater saying "rebuild on the original site" to express her demands. But the authorities rejected the proposal and the owners' corporation refused to discuss it. It was only one week before the 31 August acquisition deadline that she submitted a "letter accepting the acquisition proposal."

Ms. Yuen believes Wang Fuk Court residents have been left with no way out. She described how the two explainers she had dealt with were unable to answer her questions — their only clear objective was to follow up on whether residents would sell their flats.

Post-disaster life is like "living in someone else's home"

Since the fire, Ms. Yuen has stayed at善樓 in Tai Po and later moved to 漁映樓 in Aberdeen, paying "temporary residence fees" each month. The bed, dining table and TV cabinet originally in the unit, along with the neighbours and security guard, all serve as constant reminders of her status. She describes her life after the incident as "living in someone else's home."

Rethinking what "home" really means

Every day after work, she returns to this empty flat at eight or nine o'clock, and on holidays chooses to go to her sister's place. "Actually, after the incident, I started thinking about what 'home' means, what 'house' means. A home is supposed to be a safe place, but when this home at Wang Fuk Court was burned down…"

"Now the word 'home' feels very heavy for me"

When the reporter asked Ms. Yuen about her idea of home, she said the old phone containing photos of Wang Fuk Court was also lost in the fire, and all the memories exist only in her mind. She sighed deeply: "(Home) is not just about having a bed, a wardrobe, a bedroom, or fully equipped appliances to make it a so-called proper home. It made me rethink what the elements of a proper home really are. So I can't answer this question yet — because now the word 'home' feels very heavy for me."

Dissatisfied with officials' 'letting go' remarks

The senior officials' responses to the Wang Fuk Court fire — such as Deputy Chief Secretary Cheuk Wing-hing's 'letting go' remarks and Deputy Financial Secretary Wong Wai-lun's talk about market value — have only deepened her helplessness and anger. "The more silent you become, the less I understand," she said. "When they can actually say such callous things, what is their idea of what home means?"

A sense of being 'sold off cheap'

Recalling the moment she signed the letter accepting the acquisition, Ms. Yuen said the strongest feelings were reluctance and a sense of injustice — a feeling of being "sold off cheap" — because a home is not just its monetary value, but also a connection of emotions and memories. "The flat was something my dad and mum worked so hard for. If it really has to be taken from us for nothing, I'd be even more unwilling than accepting a 'cheap sale' now."

After signing the letter, Ms. Yuen will lose her owner status. The independent committee has been delayed until October to submit its report. Ms. Yuen says pursuing accountability is one part of it, "but as for how I personally will get through this, I can't answer. Because from the incident until now, life feels like a total loss — first, my home was burned down, and what the burning means is that it seems to have erased my entire history of growing up. A family member also died in the fire, and it was a sudden death… there's a huge hole in my heart. Can anything really fill that hole? Or will there ever be a day it heals? I don't know how to answer."
